```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ggplot2)
```

Noise is not equally autocorrelated everywhere. Voxels near large vessels
and ventricles, where cardiac and respiratory fluctuations are strongest,
usually show more autocorrelation than voxels deep in grey matter. A single
noise model for the whole brain then removes too little autocorrelation in
some regions and too much in others, and the false-positive rate moves away
from 5%: up in the first, down in the second.

fmriAR can fit a separate noise model for each parcel of a parcellation, and
can steady the estimates for small parcels by borrowing from the larger
parcels that contain them. This vignette shows both. It assumes you have
read *Getting started* (`vignette("fmriAR-introduction")`).

```{r helpers}
library(fmriAR)
set.seed(9)

TR <- 2
n_per_run <- 150
runs <- rep(1:2, each = n_per_run)

hrf <- function(t) dgamma(t, 6) - dgamma(t, 16) / 6
h <- hrf(seq(0, 30, by = TR))
event_regressor <- function(n) {
  onsets <- cumsum(sample(6:10, n, replace = TRUE))
  stim <- tabulate(onsets[onsets <= n], nbins = n)
  x <- stats::filter(stim, h / max(h), sides = 1)
  as.numeric(replace(x, is.na(x), 0))
}
cosines <- function(n, k) {
  sapply(seq_len(k), function(j) cos(pi * j * (seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n))
}
none <- matrix(0, n_per_run, 3)
X <- cbind(c(event_regressor(n_per_run), event_regressor(n_per_run)),
           runs == 1, runs == 2,
           rbind(cosines(n_per_run, 3), none),
           rbind(none, cosines(n_per_run, 3)))
colnames(X) <- c("task", "run1", "run2", paste0("drift", 1:6))

# AR(1) noise for one voxel with coefficient phi, each run simulated separately
ar1_voxel <- function(phi) {
  c(arima.sim(list(ar = phi), n = n_per_run),
    arima.sim(list(ar = phi), n = n_per_run))
}
```

## One model or one per region

The simulation has three regions of 1,500 voxels each, with AR(1)
coefficients of 0.2, 0.45 and 0.7. Every voxel is null, so every significant
voxel is a false positive.

```{r regions}
region_phi <- c(0.2, 0.45, 0.7)
region <- rep(1:3, each = 1500)
Y <- sapply(region_phi[region], ar1_voxel)
resid <- lm.fit(X, Y)$residuals
```

By default, `fit_noise()` fits one noise model to all voxels. To fit one per
region, pass `pooling = "parcel"` and a parcel label for every voxel. Pass
`multiscale = FALSE` too. Without it, and with the default `p = "auto"`,
`fit_noise()` pulls each parcel's coefficients 60% of the way toward their
average across parcels; here that would give
`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", sapply(fit_noise(resid, runs = runs, design = X, pooling = "parcel", parcels = region)$phi_by_parcel, "[", 1)), collapse = ", ")`
instead of estimates near the truth.

```{r plans}
plan_global <- fit_noise(resid, runs = runs, design = X)
plan_region <- fit_noise(resid, runs = runs, design = X, pooling = "parcel",
                         parcels = region, multiscale = FALSE)

plan_global$phi[[1]]
unlist(plan_region$phi_by_parcel)
```

Each region's estimate matches its truth. A mixture of three AR(1) processes
is not itself an AR(1), so the global search settles on a longer model whose
first coefficient lies between the three.

With a noise model per parcel, `whiten_apply()` uses the parcel labels
stored on the plan, or the ones you pass. It returns one whitened design per
parcel in `X_by`, keyed by parcel ID. The
data are whitened voxel by voxel, so `Y` keeps its shape. Fit each parcel's
voxels with that parcel's design:

```{r parcel-fit}
task_t <- function(plan, parcels = NULL) {
  w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, Y, runs = runs, parcels = parcels)
  # A global plan gives one whitened design; a parcel plan gives one per parcel
  designs <- if (is.null(w$X_by)) list(all = w$X) else w$X_by
  t <- numeric(ncol(Y))
  for (id in names(designs)) {
    cols <- if (id == "all") seq_len(ncol(Y)) else which(parcels == id)
    Xw <- designs[[id]]
    Yw <- w$Y[, cols, drop = FALSE]
    fit <- lm.fit(Xw, Yw)
    se <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(Xw, Yw, beta = fit$coefficients)$se
    t[cols] <- fit$coefficients["task", ] / se[1, ]
  }
  t
}

fp_rate <- rbind(
  global = tapply(abs(task_t(plan_global)) > 1.96, region, mean),
  `per region` = tapply(abs(task_t(plan_region, region)) > 1.96, region, mean)
)
colnames(fp_rate) <- sprintf("AR %.2f", region_phi)
knitr::kable(fp_rate, digits = 3,
             caption = "False-positive rate by region, at a nominal 5%.")
```

The global model is a compromise between the three regions. It removes too
much autocorrelation from the least autocorrelated region, whose tests
become conservative, and too little from the most autocorrelated, whose
false-positive rate rises above 5%. Separate models bring the two outer
regions back to about 5%. The middle region, which the global model already
suited, moves only by chance: with 1,500 voxels, a false-positive rate is
uncertain by about one percentage point either way.

## Small parcels and multiscale pooling

Fine parcellations have small parcels, and an estimate from a few voxels is
imprecise. Multiscale pooling steadies it. You supply the parcellation at
three nested scales, and each fine parcel's estimate is combined with the
estimates of the medium and coarse parcels that contain it.

Here 24 fine parcels of 4 voxels each sit inside 6 medium parcels, which sit
inside 3 regions of 32 voxels with the same coefficients as before. Each fine parcel's true coefficient is
its region's plus a small parcel-specific deviation (standard deviation
0.03).

```{r nested}
fine <- rep(1:24, each = 4)          # fine parcel of each voxel
medium <- (fine - 1) %/% 4 + 1       # 4 fine parcels per medium parcel
coarse <- (fine - 1) %/% 8 + 1       # 8 fine parcels per region
phi_fine <- region_phi[(1:24 - 1) %/% 8 + 1] + rnorm(24, sd = 0.03)

Y_small <- sapply(phi_fine[fine], ar1_voxel)
resid_small <- lm.fit(X, Y_small)$residuals

plan_fine <- fit_noise(resid_small, runs = runs, design = X, p = 1,
                       pooling = "parcel", parcels = fine, multiscale = FALSE)
plan_multi <- fit_noise(resid_small, runs = runs, design = X, p = 1,
                        pooling = "parcel", parcels = fine,
                        parcel_sets = list(fine = fine, medium = medium,
                                           coarse = coarse),
                        multiscale = "pacf_weighted")
```

```{r rmse}
est <- data.frame(
  parcel = 1:24,
  truth = phi_fine,
  `fine only` = sapply(plan_fine$phi_by_parcel, `[`, 1),
  multiscale = sapply(plan_multi$phi_by_parcel, `[`, 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)
est$region <- coarse[match(est$parcel, fine)]
rms_error <- function(d) {
  c(`fine only` = sqrt(mean((d$`fine only` - d$truth)^2)),
    multiscale = sqrt(mean((d$multiscale - d$truth)^2)))
}
# Root-mean-square error, overall and by region
rms <- cbind(all = rms_error(est), sapply(split(est, est$region), rms_error))
colnames(rms) <- c("all", sprintf("region %.2f", region_phi))
round(rms, 3)
```

```{r fig-parcels, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Error in the estimated AR(1) coefficient (estimate minus truth) for each of the 24 fine parcels of 4 voxels, grouped by region. Orange: the fine parcel's own estimate. Blue: after multiscale pooling. The grey line joins the two. Above each region: its true coefficient, and its root-mean-square (RMS) error before and after pooling."}
pe <- data.frame(parcel = est$parcel,
                 fine = est$`fine only` - est$truth,
                 multi = est$multiscale - est$truth)
lim <- max(abs(c(pe$fine, pe$multi)))
regions <- data.frame(parcel = c(4.5, 12.5, 20.5), y = 1.75 * lim,
                      txt = sprintf("true %.2f\nRMS %s->%s", region_phi,
                                    sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", rms["fine only", -1])),
                                    sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", rms["multiscale", -1]))))
ggplot(pe, aes(parcel)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(8.5, 16.5), linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey80") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = parcel, y = fine, yend = multi), linewidth = 0.4,
               colour = "grey65") +
  geom_point(aes(y = fine, colour = "Fine parcel only"), size = 1.7) +
  geom_point(aes(y = multi, colour = "Multiscale"), size = 1.7) +
  geom_text(data = regions, aes(y = y, label = txt), vjust = 1, size = 2.9,
            lineheight = 0.95, colour = "grey35") +
  albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Multiscale", "Fine parcel only"),
                                 guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.1 * lim, 1.75 * lim)) +
  labs(x = "Fine parcel", y = "Estimate minus truth") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

Pooling cuts the overall root-mean-square error from
`r sprintf("%.3f", rms["fine only", "all"])` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", rms["multiscale", "all"])`, but not in every region. The
price is a pull toward the larger parcels. A fine parcel whose noise
genuinely differs from its region's is drawn part of the way back, and every
fine parcel inherits whatever error the region's own estimate has: where
the region estimate is a little off, the pooled estimates of its parcels are
off in the same direction. Pooling pays most when parcels are small and
their noise varies little within a region.

## How the pooling works

Each scale's estimate is computed from the autocovariances of that parcel's
voxels, pooled across voxels without crossing run boundaries or censored
volumes. It is not computed from the parcel's average time series, whose
autocorrelation mostly reflects what the voxels have in common rather than
the noise in each one.

The three scales are then averaged with weights proportional to
$s^\beta / (1 + d)$, where $s$ is the parcel's number of voxels, $\beta$ is
0.5 by default (argument `beta`), and $d$ is the spread of voxel variances
within the parcel, measured relative to the median voxel variance so that
rescaling the data changes nothing. Larger, more homogeneous parcels get
more weight, so the region usually carries the most and the fine parcel's
own estimate the least; a smaller `beta` evens the weights and pools less.
The weights depend only on parcel size and spread, not on how far a fine
parcel's estimate is from its parents'.

`multiscale = "pacf_weighted"` averages the three scales' partial
autocorrelations, which always yields a stationary filter.
`multiscale = "acvf_pooled"` averages their autocovariances and refits.

Two defaults are worth knowing:

- With `pooling = "parcel"` and an explicit order such as `p = 1`,
  multiscale pooling is off unless you name a mode with `multiscale`.
- With `p = "auto"` and no `parcel_sets`, each parcel's partial
  autocorrelations are shrunk 60% of the way toward their average across
  parcels, whatever the parcels' sizes. Pass `multiscale = FALSE`, as above,
  to keep each parcel's own estimate.
